systemverilog-01-from-verilog.title: SystemVerilog 01 – From Verilog to SystemVerilog
systemverilog-01-from-verilog.description: Understand why SystemVerilog was introduced and how it improves RTL design and verification.

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.content:
SystemVerilog is an extension of Verilog designed to support modern hardware design and verification.

It improves readability, safety, and scalability while remaining backward compatible with Verilog.

sections.title: 2. Why SystemVerilog was Introduced
sections.content:
Verilog had limitations in large-scale designs.

• Confusing reg and wire usage
• Manual sensitivity lists caused bugs
• Limited verification capabilities

sections.title: 3. Key Improvements Over Verilog
sections.content:
SystemVerilog introduces:

• Unified design and verification language
• Richer data types like logic, bit, and int
• Specialized always blocks for clearer intent

sections.title: 4. Enhanced Procedural Blocks
sections.content: SystemVerilog introduces intent-specific always blocks.

subSections.title: always_comb (Combinational Logic)
always_ff (Sequential Logic)
always_latch (Latch Logic)

sections.title: 5. logic Data Type
sections.content:
The logic data type replaces reg in most RTL designs.

• Can be assigned in procedural blocks
• Prevents accidental multiple drivers
• Cleaner and safer than reg

sections.title: 6. Example: Sequential Logic
7. Common Beginner Mistakes
sections.content:
• Using always instead of always_ff
• Mixing blocking and non-blocking assignments
• Using wire unnecessarily instead of logic

systemverilog-02-data-types.title: SystemVerilog 02 – Data Types, Arrays, and typedef
systemverilog-02-data-types.description: Learn SystemVerilog’s rich data type system including logic, arrays, typedef, struct, and union.

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.content:
SystemVerilog provides a rich and expressive type system.

These types help write cleaner, safer, and more maintainable RTL and testbench code.

sections.title: 2. SystemVerilog Data Types
sections.content:
Commonly used SystemVerilog data types:

• logic – general-purpose 4-state signal
• bit – 2-state signal, commonly used in testbenches
• int, byte, shortint, longint for numeric data

sections.title: 3. logic vs reg vs wire
sections.content:
wire is used for continuous assignments.

reg is deprecated in SystemVerilog.

logic is the preferred replacement and should be used for most signals.
sections.example:
logic data;

assign data = a & b;

sections.title: 4. Packed Arrays
sections.content: Packed arrays represent bit vectors and are stored as a single contiguous set of bits.
sections.example: logic [15:0] instruction;

sections.title: 5. Unpacked Arrays
sections.content: Unpacked arrays represent collections of elements stored separately.
sections.example: logic buffer [0:31];

sections.title: 6. Packed and Unpacked Together
sections.content: Packed and unpacked arrays are commonly used together to model memories.

sections.title: 7. typedef
sections.content:
typedef is used to create reusable data types.

It improves readability and reduces duplication.
sections.example:
typedef logic [7:0] byte_t;

byte_t data;

sections.title: 8. struct
sections.content:
struct is used to group related signals together.

Commonly used in interfaces and testbenches.

sections.title: 9. union
sections.content:
union allows multiple interpretations of the same data.

Useful for protocol decoding and debugging.

sections.title: 10. Common Mistakes
sections.content:
• Confusing packed and unpacked array order
• Overusing wire instead of logic
• Not using typedef for repeated declarations

systemverilog-03-always-blocks.title: SystemVerilog 03 – always_comb, always_ff, always_latch
systemverilog-03-always-blocks.description: Intent-specific procedural blocks for improved correctness and readability

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.content: SystemVerilog introduces intent-specific procedural blocks that replace the traditional always block. These constructs help tools detect coding errors early and improve readability and correctness.

sections.title: 2. always_comb
sections.content:
Purpose:
Used to model purely combinational logic.

Key Rules:
- Automatically sensitive to all RHS signals
- No event control allowed (@)
- Tool checks for incomplete assignments

sections.title: Common Errors Caught
sections.content:
- Missing assignment (unintentional latch)
- Use of non-blocking assignment

sections.title: Best Practice
sections.content: Use blocking assignments (=) only.

sections.title: 3. always_ff
sections.content:
Purpose:
Used to model sequential logic (flip-flops).

Key Rules:
- Must contain exactly one clock (and optional reset)
- Only non-blocking assignments (<=) allowed
- Variable written in one always_ff block only

sections.title: Best Practice
sections.content: One always_ff per register.

sections.title: 4. always_latch
sections.content:
Purpose:
Used to explicitly model level-sensitive latches.

Key Rules:
- Incomplete assignment is intentional
- No clock edge allowed

sections.title: 5. Comparison Summary
sections.content:
- always_comb → combinational logic
- always_ff → edge-triggered storage
- always_latch → level-sensitive storage

sections.title: 6. Verification Insight
sections.content: These constructs help DV engineers quickly identify unintended latches, multiple drivers, and clocking issues.

systemverilog-05-assertions.title: SystemVerilog 05 – Introduction to SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA)
systemverilog-05-assertions.description: Verify design behavior using SystemVerilog Assertions during simulation and formal verification

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.content: Assertions verify design behavior by checking properties during simulation and formal verification.

sections.title: 2. Why Assertions?

sections.title: 4. Concurrent Assertions

uvm-01-why-uvm.title: UVM 01 – Why UVM?
uvm-01-why-uvm.description: Understand why Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) was introduced and its importance in modern verification

sections.title: 1. Overview
sections.content: Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) is a standardized verification methodology designed to handle the increasing complexity of modern digital and SoC designs.

sections.title: 2. Verification Challenges Before UVM
sections.content:
- Directed tests were hard to scale
- Low reuse between projects
- Manual checking and debugging
- Difficult coverage closure

sections.title: 3. Why UVM Was Introduced
sections.content:
- To standardize verification practices
- To promote reusable verification components
- To support constrained-random testing
- To enable coverage-driven verification

sections.title: 4. Key Benefits of UVM
sections.content:
- Reusability across blocks and projects
- Better separation of concerns
- Faster bug discovery
- Improved long-term maintainability

sections.title: 5. DV Insight
sections.content: UVM is widely used in the semiconductor industry and is a core requirement for most Design Verification roles.

uvm-02-architecture.title: UVM 02 – Testbench Architecture
uvm-02-architecture.description: Understand the layered and hierarchical structure of a UVM testbench

sections.title: 1. Overview
sections.content: UVM testbenches use a layered and hierarchical architecture to improve scalability, reuse, and readability.

sections.title: 2. Top-Level Components
sections.content:
- Test: Controls configuration and sequences
- Environment: Groups agents and scoreboards

sections.title: 3. Agent Structure
sections.content:
- Active Agent: Sequencer, Driver, Monitor
- Passive Agent: Monitor only

sections.title: 4. Data Flow
sections.content: Sequences generate transactions, drivers drive DUT signals, monitors observe behavior, and scoreboards verify correctness.

sections.title: 5. DV Insight
sections.content: Understanding the architecture is critical for debugging and extending UVM environments.

uvm-03-transactions-sequences.title: UVM 03 – Transactions, Sequences, Drivers
uvm-03-transactions-sequences.description: Learn how stimulus is generated and driven in UVM

sections.title: 1. Overview
sections.content: UVM abstracts stimulus generation from signal-level activity using transactions and sequences.

sections.title: 2. Transactions (Sequence Items)
sections.content:
- Represent high-level data packets
- Timing independent
- Easily randomized

sections.title: 3. Sequences
sections.content: Sequences generate ordered streams of transactions that model realistic traffic scenarios.

sections.title: 4. Sequencer and Driver Interaction
sections.content: The sequencer arbitrates sequences while the driver converts transactions into pin-level signals.

sections.title: 5. DV Insight
sections.content: This abstraction improves stimulus reuse and simplifies verification.

uvm-04-monitors-scoreboards.title: UVM 04 – Monitors and Scoreboards
uvm-04-monitors-scoreboards.description: Learn how checking and self-verification is done in UVM

sections.title: 1. Overview
sections.content: Monitors and scoreboards enable automated and self-checking verification.

sections.title: 2. Monitor Responsibilities
sections.content:
- Observe DUT signals passively
- Convert signals to transactions
- Send data using analysis ports

sections.title: 3. Scoreboard Responsibilities
sections.content:
- Compare expected vs actual behavior
- Detect mismatches
- Report errors clearly

sections.title: 4. Benefits of Self-Checking
sections.content:
- Reduced manual debugging
- Faster validation
- Reliable regression testing

sections.title: 5. DV Insight
sections.content: Self-checking environments are mandatory in production-quality verification.

uvm-05-mini-environment.title: UVM 05 – Mini UVM Environment
uvm-05-mini-environment.description: Understand a complete but minimal UVM testbench and how core UVM components work together

sections.title: 1. What is a Mini UVM Environment?
sections.content: A Mini UVM Environment is a simplified but complete UVM testbench used to demonstrate the interaction between core UVM components without unnecessary complexity.

sections.title: 2. Components Used
sections.content:
Test: Controls configuration and starts sequences
Environment: Container that holds agents and scoreboards
Agent: Represents one DUT interface
Sequencer: Controls transaction flow
Driver: Drives transactions to DUT signals
Monitor: Observes DUT signals
Scoreboard: Checks correctness of DUT behavior

sections.title: 3. Component Connection Structure
sections.content:
Test → Environment → Agent → (Sequencer → Driver → DUT)
Monitor → Scoreboard

sections.title: 4. Basic Execution Flow
sections.content:
1. Test creates the environment
2. Test starts a sequence 3. Sequence generates transactions 4. Driver drives signals to the DUT 5. Monitor observes DUT activity 6. Scoreboard compares expected and actual results

sections.title: 5. UVM Phases Used
sections.content:
- build_phase: create components
- connect_phase: connect TLM ports
- run_phase: execute stimulus and checking
- report_phase: summarize results

sections.title: 6. What This Mini Environment Does Not Include
sections.content:
- Coverage collection
- Advanced configuration database usage
- Virtual sequences
- Multiple agents or interfaces

sections.title: 7. Why This Matters in Design Verification
sections.content: This mini environment forms the foundation of all real-world UVM testbenches and helps verification engineers understand stimulus flow, checking, and component interaction.

sections.title: 8. Summary
sections.content: A Mini UVM Environment demonstrates the complete UVM flow in its simplest form, making it ideal for learning, debugging, and interview preparation.
